 "screeningLimitations": "A single survey at one time point, with self-report measures, so predictors cannot be shown to cause profile membership and common-method bias is possible. Analytic sample sizes differ between tables (458 in Table 4, 521 in Table 5).",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the four profiles as distinct types of performers to be sorted, when the authors found the profiles differ mainly in overall level and the predictors were measured at the same time as the outcomes.",
 "paper": {

   "doi": "10.1123/jsep.2016-0293",
   "abstract": "Factor mixture analysis of 535 sport performers' responses to demanding competitive encounters over the past month, using subjective performance, vitality and positive affect. Four profiles emerged, and resilient qualities, psychological skills, need satisfaction and frustration, and challenge appraisal predicted profile membership.",
   "tldr": "Competitive athletes who thrived in demanding events rated both their performance and well-being highly, and this group could be identified statistically. Resilience, psychological skills, need satisfaction and challenge appraisal were linked to thriving, so these are candidate targets for practice.",
   "methods": "Questionnaire on performance and well-being in demanding competitions over the past month. Measures included self-rated performance (0 to 10), subjective vitality, positive affect, resilient qualities, psychological skills use, social support, coach need-supportive and need-thwarting behavior, challenge and threat appraisal, and basic psychological needs. Factor mixture models with one to six profiles were compared on fit and interpretability.",
   "findings": "Four profiles were retained: thriving (27.9%), above average (25.0%), below average (39.9%) and low functioning (7.3%). Higher resilient qualities were linked to lower odds of membership in each of the other three profiles relative to thriving. Higher need satisfaction lowered those odds, and higher need frustration raised the odds of the below-average profile. Challenge appraisal lowered the odds of the low-functioning profile. Social support and coach behaviors did not predict membership.",
   "limitations": "The analysis is data-driven and cross-sectional, and the authors call for replication. Thriving is measured with single-item self-rated performance, and the thriving and above-average profiles overlap on that item. The sample is mostly male, mostly British and mostly at regional or senior level, with only 0.7% professional.",
   "practicalImplications": "Practitioners who want to support thriving could work on resilient qualities, psychological skills, the satisfaction of autonomy, competence and relatedness needs, and how athletes appraise competition as a challenge.    "athleteDev": "Most of the sample were adult senior performers, although ages from 16 upward were included. The study offers a framework for thinking about resilience and psychological skills in athletes, but it does not test whether building these skills raises thriving over time.",
   "rtp": "The study does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, and its participants were excluded if injury kept them from competing. It cannot be used to judge readiness to return after injury or to predict re-injury."

 Performers’ Responses to Competitive Encounters
 Daniel J. Brown,1,2 Rachel Arnold,1 Martyn Standage,1 and David Fletcher3
 1
 University of Bath; 2University of Portsmouth; 3Loughborough University
 Although considerable research exists on performers’ responses to sporting encounters, little is known about
 thriving in sport contexts. The current study examined if distinct response patterns existed between sport
 performers who thrived in competitive encounters compared with those who did not. Participants were 535
 sport performers (134 women; Mage = 23.60 years, SDage = 8.08; Mcompeting = 11.84 years, SDcompeting = 7.11).
 Results of factor mixture analysis supported a four-proﬁle solution comprising a thriving group (n = 146), a
 low-functioning group (n = 38), and two groups characterized by scores marginally above (n = 131) and below
 (n = 209) the sample mean. Proﬁle membership was found to be predicted by personal enablers (viz., personal
 resilient qualities, psychological skills use) and process variables (viz., basic psychological need satisfaction
 and frustration, challenge appraisal). This examination of thriving in sport performers offers signiﬁcant
 implications for research and practice.

{
 "id": "Q63",
 "sourceFile": "Throwing cold water on muscle growth - A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Throwing cold water on muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of eight randomized trials (4 to 12 weeks; young adults aged 20 to 26, mostly men, trained and untrained) comparing resistance training with cold water immersion given after each session against resistance training with passive, active or sham recovery. The comparative pooled effect favored resistance training alone for muscle growth (cSMD -0.22, 95% CrI -0.47 to 0.04), with a posterior probability of 0.957 that the difference was below zero.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Overall quality is fair to poor (mean SMART-LD score 9.8 of 20; mean Downs and Black score 18.4 of 29), trials are small (8 to 21 participants), and only one included women. No trial included adolescents or older adults, and the samples were healthy young adults rather than athletes. The 95% credible interval for the main comparison includes zero.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the pooled result as proof that cold water immersion blunts muscle growth in athletes, when the interval crosses zero, the trials are small and of fair to poor quality, and the samples were healthy young adults rather than athletes.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Piñero A, et al. Throwing cold water on muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-13.",
   "doi": "10.1002/ejsc.12074",
   "abstract": "Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of eight randomized trials comparing resistance training with cold water immersion after each session against resistance training alone. The pooled comparison favored resistance training alone for muscle growth, but the credible interval included zero, and study quality was mostly fair to poor.",
   "tldr": "Cold water immersion straight after resistance training may slightly reduce muscle growth compared with training alone. The authors urge caution because the trials are small and of fair to poor quality, and the finding applies only to immersion within about 15 minutes of training.",
   "methods": "PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to 24 February 2023, with reference-list checks. The review was preregistered and followed PRISMA. Eight randomized trials were pooled with Bayesian random-effects models. Study quality was rated with two tools: SMART-LD, developed for resistance training research, and the Downs and Black checklist.",
   "findings": "Uncontrolled effects showed resistance training alone produced muscle growth (SMD 0.36, 95% CrI 0.10 to 0.61), while cold water immersion plus resistance training produced small-to-negligible growth (SMD 0.14, 95% CrI -0.08 to 0.36). The comparative effect favored resistance training alone (cSMD -0.22, 95% CrI -0.47 to 0.04). Meta-regression found no clear moderation by training status, study duration or training frequency.",
   "limitations": "Muscle growth was measured with different methods (DXA, biopsy, ultrasound, MRI and circumference), and training programs varied, with few multi-joint or whole-body protocols. Nutrition was rarely tracked, and cold water timing and temperature varied little across studies. The findings apply to immersion within 15 minutes after exercise, not to cryotherapy or intermittent use.",
   "practicalImplications": "Athletes whose goal is maximal muscle size may avoid cold water immersion immediately after resistance sessions, and may consider the timing and frequency of any cooling. The authors note that cryotherapy and intermittent cooling were not tested for long-term muscle growth.",
   "athleteDev": "The trials used young adults, not youth athletes, and included no adolescents. The review therefore cannot show whether post-session cold water immersion affects muscle growth in developing athletes.",
   "rtp": "The review excluded trials with musculoskeletal injury and studies no return-to-sport outcomes. It cannot show whether cold water immersion helps or delays rehabilitation or the return to training."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q64",
 "sourceFile": "Thursday Night Footballs impact on  all cause injuries in NFL players during 2012-2017.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Thursday Night Football's impact on all-cause injuries in NFL players during 2012-2017' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective analysis of weekly NFL injury reports and injured reserve data for the 2012 to 2017 regular seasons, covering 1,211 weekend games and 69 Thursday Night Football games. The authors counted 9,621 all-cause injuries, with rates of 7,598 per 1,000 athletic exposures on weekends and 6,072 per 1,000 on Thursdays (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.95 to 0.98). Thursday games did not show higher injury rates despite shorter rest.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Injury reports do not show whether an injury happened in a game or in practice, so the authors assumed all listed injuries were game injuries. The reports lack injury type, severity and time lost, the Thursday sample is small (69 games), and follow-up is short-term.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the lower Thursday rate as proof that short recovery is safe for players, when the data cannot separate game from practice injuries and include no severity or time-loss measures.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2019,
   "citation": "Baker HP, Lee KY-H, Dayton SR, Terry M, Tjong VK. Thursday Night Football's impact on all-cause injuries in NFL players during 2012-2017. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2019.",
   "doi": "10.1080/00913847.2019.1587565",
   "abstract": "Compared all-cause injury rates in NFL regular-season weekend games and Thursday Night Football games from 2012 to 2017, using weekly injury reports and injured reserve data. Thursday games had a slightly lower rate despite shorter recovery, and the authors conclude that dropping them is unlikely to lower injury rates.",
   "tldr": "NFL Thursday night games, which give players about three days of rest, had a slightly lower all-cause injury rate than weekend games from 2012 to 2017. Injury reports cannot show whether injuries happened in practice or in games, so this is a short-term signal rather than proof that short rest is safe.",
   "methods": "Retrospective analysis. Weekly injury reports and injured reserve lists were collected for all 32 teams across five regular seasons. An injury was any reported injury not previously on a report. Rates per 1,000 athletic exposures, where one game equals one exposure, were compared using relative risk with 95% confidence intervals.",
   "findings": "There were 9,621 all-cause injuries overall: 9,202 during weekend games (rate 7,598 per 1,000 exposures) and 419 during Thursday games (rate 6,072 per 1,000 exposures). The relative risk was 0.97 (95% CI 0.95 to 0.98), which the authors describe as statistically significant.",
   "limitations": "The authors assumed injuries on the reports happened in games, which cannot be verified from the data. Reports lack injury type, severity and time lost, and no long-term outcomes were measured. The Discussion calls the difference a 3% absolute risk reduction, but the reported figure is a relative risk of 0.97, so the wording should be read with care.",
   "practicalImplications": "On this evidence, medical staff should not assume that Thursday games raise all-cause injury risk. The authors suggest that changing the schedule is unlikely to change injury rates, so prevention effort may be better spent elsewhere. Injury records should include type and time lost so that future schedule comparisons can be sharper.",
   "athleteDev": "The study covers professional NFL players only, so it says nothing about how short recovery affects injury or development in younger players.",
   "rtp": "The study does not report time lost, return to play or re-injury, so it cannot show whether short recovery between games affects how quickly players return. It counts new injuries only and says nothing about return timing."
 }
}

import json, os
W = "/Users/kristinarash/Library/Caches/sportsci-batch-100"
inputs = json.load(open(f"{W}/inputs.json"))
items = inputs if isinstance(inputs, list) else inputs.get("items", inputs)
src = {it["id"]: it["sourceFile"] for it in items}

def load(i):
    return json.load(open(f"{W}/drafts/{i}.json"))

def save(i, d, status, changes, concerns, prio):
    d["sourceFile"] = src[i]
    d["verification"] = {"status": status, "changes": changes,
                         "residualConcerns": concerns, "spotCheckPriority": prio}
    for k, v in d.items():
        if isinstance(v, str) and "—" in v:
            raise SystemExit(f"em dash in {i}.{k}")
    if d.get("paper"):
        for k, v in d["paper"].items():
            if isinstance(v, str) and "—" in v:
                raise SystemExit(f"em dash in {i}.paper.{k}")
    json.dump(d, open(f"{W}/verified/{i}.json", "w"), indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)

# Q57
d = load("Q57"); p = d["paper"]
p["findings"] = ("Animal and in vitro studies report that CBD and THC reduce pain, inflammation and neuronal damage in some models. "
    "The review reports preclinical and some clinical support for cannabinoids in osteoarthritis but states that CBD is not an FDA-approved treatment of choice, and for concussion it states that no trials exist. "
    "One simulated public-speaking study found 300 mg of CBD reduced anxiety more than 150 mg or 600 mg, a separate study found 600 mg increased anxiety in a high-trait-paranoid group, and cardiovascular findings were inconsistent and measured at rest rather than during exercise.")
save("Q57", d, "CORRECTED",
 ["paper.findings: implied the 300 mg and 600 mg anxiety results came from one study -> attributed to two separate studies (Linares et al. U-shaped dose response; 'Hundal et al. (52) found that 600 mg of CBD caused increased anxiety in paranoid groups'); trimmed to 3 sentences"],
 "Clinically sensitive (cannabinoid use, concussion). No own DOI printed; operator should verify DOI externally.", "high")

# Q58
d = load("Q58")
save("Q58", d, "VERIFIED", [],
 "", "normal")

# Q59
d = load("Q59"); p = d["paper"]
p["methods"] = ("Review of laboratory and field studies, using a described search of PubMed and EBSCO from inception to January 2016, reference-list checks and broad inclusion criteria (English, peer-reviewed, healthy youth and adult athletes). "
    "No pooled analysis or formal quality scoring is reported.")
p["findings"] = ("Heat illness and heat stroke are more common in football than in other sports, and most cases occur in preseason practice. "
    "Linemen have higher body mass and body fat, lower surface area to mass ratios and lower aerobic capacity, and show higher core temperatures and sweating rates than backs. "
    "Full or partial uniforms raise sweating rates compared with shorts, with no difference between full and half pads; sweat sodium concentration is similar to other sports, and mean body mass loss in most field studies was about 2% or less.")
save("Q59", d, "CORRECTED",
 ["paper.methods: called it a narrative review, inconsistent with studyDesign -> described as a review with a described search and stated inclusion criteria ('The literature search was conducted using PubMed and EBSCO databases')",
  "paper.findings: 'Full pads raise sweating rates compared with shorts' omitted that full and partial uniforms did not differ -> added ('no differences in sweating rate were found between full and partial uniforms'); condensed to 3 sentences"],
 "studyDesign kept as Systematic Review / Meta-analysis per library precedent (described database search and inclusion criteria), although the paper is labelled a review article with narrative synthesis. Authors are Gatorade Sports Science Institute employees.", "normal")

# Q60
d = load("Q60"); p = d["paper"]
p["findings"] = ("Median mental fatigue ranged from 0 to 70.5 across the three coaches, with elevated ratings in weeks 8 and 12, after interstate double-header preseason matches, and in week 10, after a preseason tournament. "
    "Mental fatigue was inversely related to readiness to perform (r = -.44, P = .002) and positively related to physical fatigue (r = .67), while physical fatigue was not related to readiness (r = -.19, P = .208). "
    "The authors interpret the salivary cortisol and alpha-amylase values as indicating psychophysiological stress in all three staff members.")
p["practicalImplications"] = ("The authors recommend educating staff about mental fatigue and strategies to manage or acutely reduce it. "
    "Elevated ratings followed travel for preseason matches and a preseason tournament, so those periods may be worth watching, although the study did not test any workload change.")
save("Q60", d, "CORRECTED",
 ["paper.findings: added the week 10 elevation and the nonsignificant physical fatigue-readiness correlation ('r = -.19 [-.45 to .1], P = .208'); salivary stress framed as the authors' interpretation",
  "paper.practicalImplications: 'highest ratings' after travel periods overstated the data -> 'elevated ratings' ('Elevated ratings were observed in weeks 8 and 12'), and noted no workload change was tested"],
 "The reported CI for the mental-physical fatigue correlation (r = .67 [-.45 to .1]) appears to be a copy error in the source.", "normal")

# Q61
d = load("Q61"); p = d["paper"]
p["practicalImplications"] = ("The authors suggest that management of players with a past hamstring strain could include interventions that alter lumbopelvic fascia and muscle stiffness. "
    "This study tested no intervention, so it does not show that such exercises change stiffness or reduce re-injury.")
save("Q61", d, "CORRECTED",
 ["paper.practicalImplications: presented assessing and exercising lumbar tissue as staff advice -> framed as the authors' suggestion with no intervention tested ('Management of athletes with a previous hamstring injury could include exercises or interventions that alter stiffness')"],
 "Sex is stated as male only for the uninjured group ('Thirteen male soccer players'); the injured group's sex is not explicitly stated. Table 1 numbering is irregular (participant 4 listed twice, 9 missing). Reported partial eta squared values (0.967 to 0.999) are implausibly high.", "normal")

# Q62
d = load("Q62"); p = d["paper"]
p["findings"] = ("Four profiles were retained: thriving (27.9%), above average (25.0%), below average (39.9%) and low functioning (7.3%). "
    "Higher resilient qualities lowered the odds of membership in each of the other three profiles relative to thriving, and greater psychological skills use lowered the odds of the below-average and low-functioning profiles. "
    "Higher need satisfaction lowered the odds of all three, higher need frustration raised the odds of the below-average profile, challenge appraisal lowered the odds of the low-functioning profile, and social support and coach behaviors did not predict membership.")
p["limitations"] = ("The analysis is data-driven and cross-sectional, and the authors call for replication. "
    "Subjective performance is a single self-rated item, and the thriving and above-average profiles may overlap on it. "
    "The sample is mostly male, mostly British and mostly at regional or senior level, with only 0.7% professional.")
save("Q62", d, "CORRECTED",
 ["paper.findings: omitted the psychological skills use result -> added (OR 0.660 below average, 0.354 low functioning vs thriving)",
  "paper.limitations: 'Thriving is measured with single-item self-rated performance' -> thriving used three indicators; only subjective performance is a single item ('satisfaction with their sporting performance over the past month on an 11-point scale')"],
 "", "normal")

# Q63
d = load("Q63"); p = d["paper"]
d["populations"] = ["Adult / Recreational"]
d["screeningLimitations"] = ("Quality was fair to poor by the SMART-LD tool (mean 9.8 of 20) but good to fair by the Downs and Black checklist (mean 18.4 of 29), trials are small (8 to 21 participants), and only one included women. "
    "No trial included adolescents or older adults, the samples were healthy trained or untrained young adults rather than athletes, and the 95% credible interval for the main comparison includes zero.")
p["citation"] = ("Piñero A, Burke R, Augustin F, Mohan AE, DeJesus K, Sapuppo M, et al. Throwing cold water on muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-13.")
p["rtp"] = ("The review excluded trials of people with musculoskeletal injury and included no return-to-sport outcomes. "
    "It cannot show whether cold water immersion helps or delays rehabilitation or the return to training.")
save("Q63", d, "CORRECTED",
 ["screeningLimitations: 'Overall quality is fair to poor' applied to both tools -> SMART-LD fair to poor, Downs and Black good to fair ('The frequently used Downs and Black checklist indicated that the included studies were generally of good to fair quality')",
  "populations: Mixed / Unspecified -> Adult / Recreational (healthy trained and untrained young adults aged 20 to 26, not athletes)",
  "paper.citation: 'Piñero A, et al.' -> first six authors listed before et al. as printed",
  "paper.rtp: grammar fix ('studies no return-to-sport outcomes' -> 'included no return-to-sport outcomes')"],
 "", "normal")

# Q64
d = load("Q64"); p = d["paper"]
d["populations"] = ["Professional / Elite"]
d["screeningLimitations"] = ("Injury reports do not show whether an injury happened in a game or in practice, so the authors assumed all listed injuries were game injuries. "
    "The reports lack injury type, severity and time lost, the Thursday sample is small (69 games), and the reported relative risk (0.97) does not match the reported rates, which imply a ratio near 0.80.")
p["limitations"] = ("The authors assumed injuries on the reports happened in games, which cannot be verified, and reports lack injury type, severity and time lost. "
    "The reported relative risk of 0.97 does not match the rates in Table 1 (6,072 vs 7,598 per 1,000 exposures, a ratio of about 0.80), the Discussion calls it a 3% absolute risk reduction, and weekend injuries are given as 9,202 in the text but 9,201 in the table.")
p["practicalImplications"] = ("These data do not support the view that Thursday games raise all-cause injury counts. "
    "They cannot rule out effects on injury severity, time lost or practice injuries, so they should not be used alone to judge whether three days of rest is enough.")
save("Q64", d, "CORRECTED",
 ["populations: removed 'Injured Athletes' -> sample is all NFL players on injury reports across seasons, not an injured cohort",
  "screeningLimitations / paper.limitations: added that the reported RR 0.97 is inconsistent with the reported rates (419/69 = 6,072 vs 9,201/1211 = 7,598 per 1,000, ratio about 0.80) and the 9,202 vs 9,201 count mismatch",
  "paper.practicalImplications: removed unsupported advice ('prevention effort may be better spent elsewhere', record-keeping advice) -> limited to what the rate comparison can and cannot show"],
 "The relative risk and its CI as printed (0.97, 0.95 to 0.98) conflict with the printed injury rates; a reviewer should check which figure is correct before citing.", "high")
print("ok")
